home.title: Compassionate care for your digestive health
home.text: From colon cancer screening to heartburn, liver disease and IBS, Dr. Kurt Vernon, "The GI Guy," has cared for patients across the Greater Raleigh area for more than 30 years.

about.title: About Us
about.text:
At The GI Guy, we are dedicated to expert gastroenterology care with a compassionate, holistic approach. Led by Dr. Kurt Vernon, our practice has served the Greater Raleigh area for over 30 years from two offices in Fuquay-Varina and Dunn, NC.

We use modern endoscopy equipment and create a unique atmosphere where patients come first.

Our approach looks at your health as a whole: we provide education, incorporate nutrition and lifestyle, and recommend only the best quality products.

values.title: Personalized care
values.text: We take the time to understand each patient's needs and build a treatment plan around your goals.

values.title: Advanced technology
values.text: Modern equipment for accurate, minimally invasive procedures.

values.title: Education and support
values.text: We want you to leave informed, with the knowledge to make good decisions about your health.

about.insurance: We accept Medicare, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Cigna, Aetna, UnitedHealthcare, Wellpath and many other plans. Please call us to confirm your coverage.
about.wellnessText: Your digestive system is tied to your health as a whole, so we take an integrated wellness approach. Browse the doctor-approved wellness products in our [GI Guy Metagenics store](https://giguy.metagenics.com/), and ask Dr. Vernon or our staff about questions and recommendations.

doctor.name: Kurt Vernon, MD, FACG
doctor.quote: The secret to successful treatment is personalized care. I always take the time to work one-on-one with patients during their program. My patients know that I am always available for them. I explain everything I do and encourage patients to ask questions. In the end, they aren't just healed, they're educated, too.
doctor.bio:
Kurt Vernon, MD is a board-certified gastroenterologist and a Fellow of the American College of Gastroenterology, the American College of Physicians and the American Anti-Aging Academy, with more than 30 years of experience.

Dr. Vernon has the expertise and advanced technology to accurately diagnose and treat a wide range of colon, liver, digestive and rectal conditions, including cancer screening, abdominal pain, ulcers, irritable bowel syndrome and heartburn/reflux. Add in his bedside manner and caring personality, and it's easy to see why over 90% of his patients come from referrals. Many of our patients are physicians and medical professionals themselves.

Dr. Vernon is board-certified in internal medicine and gastroenterology by the American Board of Internal Medicine, and he continually works to refine his skills and use the latest medical techniques.

services.title: Colonoscopy
services.summary: Early detection and prevention of colon cancer.
services.points:
Finds and removes precancerous polyps before they become cancer
Helps diagnose abdominal pain, rectal bleeding and changes in bowel habits
services.what: A colonoscopy is an exam of the inside of the colon and rectum. The doctor uses a long, thin, flexible tube with a camera on the end. Polyps can be removed and tissue samples can be taken during the same exam.
services.why:
Screening for colon cancer starting at age 45 for average-risk adults
Finding and removing polyps before they can become cancer
Checking the cause of rectal bleeding or black stools
Looking into changes in bowel habits, diarrhea, or belly pain
Follow-up after a positive stool test such as Cologuard
Monitoring inflammatory bowel disease or a history of polyps
services.prep: Your colon must be completely clean so the doctor can see the lining clearly. This usually means a clear liquid diet the day before and drinking a bowel prep solution that causes diarrhea. You may need to change or stop some medicines, such as blood thinners or diabetes medicines, but only as directed. The office will give you specific instructions, so follow them closely and call with any questions.
services.expect: You will receive sedation through an IV, so most people sleep through the exam or remember very little. You lie on your side while the doctor gently guides the scope through the colon and looks at the lining. Any polyps found can usually be removed during the exam. The procedure itself often takes about 30 to 60 minutes, but plan to be at the center longer for check-in and recovery.
services.after: You must have an adult drive you home because of the sedation, and you should not drive, work, or make important decisions for the rest of the day. You may feel bloated or have gas for a few hours. Dr. Vernon will share what was seen after the exam, and biopsy or polyp results are usually ready within a week or two.

services.title: EGD (upper endoscopy)
services.summary: Diagnosis and treatment of upper digestive problems.
services.points:
Examines the esophagus, stomach and upper small intestine
Diagnoses acid reflux, ulcers and upper GI bleeding
Allows biopsy or treatment during the same procedure
services.what: An EGD, or upper endoscopy, is an exam of the upper digestive tract. It looks at the esophagus, stomach, and the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). The doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera that passes through the mouth. Tissue samples can be taken and some problems can be treated during the exam.
services.why:
Heartburn or acid reflux that does not get better
Trouble or pain with swallowing
Upper belly pain, nausea, or vomiting
Signs of bleeding, such as vomiting blood, black stools, or anemia
Checking for ulcers, H. pylori, celiac disease, or Barrett's esophagus
Unexplained weight loss
services.prep: Your stomach needs to be empty, so you will usually be asked not to eat or drink for several hours before the exam. You may need to adjust some medicines, such as blood thinners or diabetes medicines, only as directed. The office will give you specific instructions about timing and medicines. Plan to have an adult drive you home.
services.expect: You will receive sedation through an IV to keep you comfortable, and your throat may be numbed. You lie on your side, and a mouth guard protects your teeth. The doctor gently passes the scope through your mouth and looks at the lining, and may take small tissue samples. The exam usually takes about 10 to 20 minutes.
services.after: You must have an adult drive you home and should rest for the rest of the day. You may have a mild sore throat or feel bloated for a short time. Dr. Vernon will review what was seen, and biopsy results are usually ready within a week or two.

services.title: Capsule endoscopy
services.summary: A detailed look at the small intestine, no scope needed.
services.points:
You swallow a small camera capsule
Captures detailed images of the small intestine
Useful for finding bleeding, polyps and inflammation
services.what: Capsule endoscopy uses a tiny camera inside a pill-sized capsule that you swallow. As it moves through your digestive tract, it takes thousands of pictures, mainly of the small intestine. The pictures are sent to a small recorder you wear. This test can see parts of the small intestine that standard scopes cannot easily reach.
services.why:
Finding the source of bleeding when EGD and colonoscopy do not show a cause
Checking for the cause of low iron or anemia
Looking for Crohn's disease in the small intestine
Checking for small bowel polyps or tumors
Evaluating celiac disease in some cases
services.prep: You will usually follow a clear liquid diet and may take a bowel prep before the test so the pictures are clear. You will need to stop eating and drinking for several hours before you swallow the capsule. Tell the office if you have trouble swallowing, a history of bowel blockage, or a pacemaker or other implanted device. The office will give you specific instructions.
services.expect: Sensors or a belt are placed on your belly and connected to a recorder you wear. You swallow the capsule with water, and no sedation is needed. You can usually go about light daily activities while the capsule takes pictures for several hours. The office will tell you when you can drink and eat again and when to return the recorder.
services.after: The capsule usually passes in a bowel movement within a day or a few days and does not need to be collected. Call the office right away if you have belly pain, bloating, or vomiting, or if you are not sure the capsule has passed. The pictures take time to review, and Dr. Vernon will share the results at a follow-up.

services.title: Flexible sigmoidoscopy
services.summary: Quick screening of the lower colon and rectum.
services.points:
Screens the lower colon for polyps and other problems
Typically takes less than 30 minutes with minimal preparation
services.what: A flexible sigmoidoscopy is an exam of the rectum and the lower part of the colon, called the sigmoid colon. The doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera. It looks at less of the colon than a colonoscopy. Polyps can be removed and tissue samples can be taken during the exam.
services.why:
Checking the cause of bright red rectal bleeding
Looking into diarrhea or changes in bowel habits
Checking for inflammation in the lower colon
Monitoring inflammatory bowel disease in some cases
Screening for colon cancer in some patients
services.prep: The lower colon must be clean for the exam. This often means using one or more enemas before the test, and sometimes a lighter diet the day before. Some medicines may need to be adjusted only as directed. The office will give you specific instructions.
services.expect: Many people have this exam with little or no sedation, though sedation may be used in some cases. You lie on your side while the doctor gently passes the scope into the rectum and lower colon. You may feel pressure or cramping as air is used to open the colon. The exam usually takes about 10 to 20 minutes.
services.after: If you did not have sedation, you can usually go back to normal activities the same day. If you did have sedation, you will need an adult to drive you home. Biopsy results are usually ready within a week or two, and a full colonoscopy may be recommended if polyps or other problems are found.

services.title: Esophageal dilation
services.points:
Gently widens narrowed areas of the esophagus
Treats strictures caused by reflux (GERD) or injury
Often brings immediate relief
services.what: Esophageal dilation is a procedure that gently stretches a narrowed area of the esophagus. It is usually done during an upper endoscopy (EGD). The doctor uses a small balloon or a tapered tube called a dilator to widen the narrowing. This can make it easier for food and liquid to pass.
services.why:
Trouble swallowing caused by a narrowing in the esophagus
Scar tissue from long-term acid reflux
A ring or web in the esophagus
Narrowing from eosinophilic esophagitis
Food getting stuck in the esophagus
services.prep: Preparation is the same as for an upper endoscopy. You will usually need to stop eating and drinking for several hours before the procedure. Some medicines, especially blood thinners, may need to be adjusted only as directed. The office will give you specific instructions and you will need an adult to drive you home.
services.expect: You will receive sedation through an IV. The doctor first looks at the esophagus with the scope, then gently widens the narrowed area with a balloon or dilator. The whole procedure usually takes about 15 to 30 minutes. Some people need more than one dilation over time to get the best result.
services.after: You will need an adult to drive you home and should rest for the day. A mild sore throat or chest discomfort is common for a short time, and the office will tell you when you can eat and what to start with. Call right away or seek emergency care for severe chest or neck pain, fever, trouble breathing, or vomiting blood.

services.title: Hemorrhoid treatment
services.summary: Minimally invasive relief with the CRH O'Regan System.
services.points:
Quick, in-office banding with little to no downtime for most patients
Lasting relief from pain, bleeding and discomfort
services.what: Dr. Vernon treats internal hemorrhoids in the office using the CRH O'Regan System. This method uses a small rubber band placed around the base of an internal hemorrhoid. The band cuts off the blood supply, so the hemorrhoid shrinks and falls off, usually within a few days. It uses gentle suction and does not require metal clamps.
services.why:
Internal hemorrhoids that bleed
Hemorrhoids that bulge out during bowel movements
Itching, irritation, or discomfort that does not get better with home care
An option to treat hemorrhoids in the office instead of in an operating room
services.prep: Most people need little or no special preparation. You can usually eat normally and drive yourself to and from the visit. Tell the office about all your medicines, especially blood thinners. The office will give you any specific instructions you need.
services.expect: The treatment is done in the office and usually takes only a few minutes. No sedation is needed. Dr. Vernon gently places a small band on one hemorrhoid at a time. Most people need a few visits, spaced a couple of weeks apart, to treat all the hemorrhoids.
services.after: Most people go right back to normal activities the same day. You may feel mild pressure or fullness for a day or two, and you may notice a small amount of bleeding when the band falls off. Eating more fiber and drinking water can help prevent hemorrhoids from coming back; call the office for severe pain, heavy bleeding, fever, or trouble passing urine.

services.title: Cologuard® screening
services.summary: A no-prep, at-home stool DNA test for colon cancer.
services.points:
An option for average-risk patients who don't want a colonoscopy
A positive result needs a follow-up colonoscopy
services.what: Cologuard is a colon cancer screening test you do at home. It checks a stool sample for certain DNA changes and tiny amounts of blood that can be signs of colon cancer or large polyps. It is an option for some adults at average risk who have no symptoms. Dr. Vernon's practice can help you decide if it is the right test for you.
services.why:
Colon cancer screening for average-risk adults age 45 and older
A non-invasive option that does not require a bowel prep or sedation
An option for people who are not ready for a colonoscopy
Can be done privately at home
services.prep: No bowel prep, diet changes, or time off work are needed. The kit is shipped to your home after your doctor orders it. Read the instructions in the kit before you start. Cologuard is not the right test if you have symptoms, a history of polyps or colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or a strong family history, so talk with the doctor first.
services.expect: You collect a stool sample at home using the container in the kit and follow the steps to add the preservative and seal it. Then you place the sample in the box and mail it back using the included shipping label. Send the sample back soon after you collect it, as the kit instructions explain. The lab tests the sample and sends the results to your doctor.
services.after: Your doctor's office will contact you with the results. A negative result means no signs were found, and you will need to repeat screening in the future, usually every three years. A positive result does not mean you have cancer, but it does mean you need a colonoscopy to look for the cause.

services.title: GI consultations
services.summary: Evaluation and ongoing care for digestive conditions.
services.points:
Heartburn, IBS, IBD, liver disease, abdominal pain and more
Nutrition, lifestyle and wellness guidance as part of your plan
services.what: A GI consultation is an office visit with Dr. Vernon to talk about your digestive health. It may be for new symptoms, a long-term condition, a referral from another doctor, or colon cancer screening. The visit is a chance to understand what is going on and make a plan together.
services.why:
New or ongoing digestive symptoms, such as belly pain, heartburn, or changes in bowel habits
A referral from your primary care doctor
Planning colon cancer screening
Abnormal blood tests, such as liver tests or low iron
Managing a long-term condition such as IBS, IBD, or fatty liver
Nutrition and lifestyle guidance for digestive health
services.prep: Bring a list of all your medicines, vitamins, and supplements, along with your insurance card and photo ID. Bring or have sent any prior records, lab results, imaging reports, and reports from past endoscopies or colonoscopies. Write down your symptoms, when they started, and any questions you have. Know your family history of colon cancer, polyps, or other digestive diseases if you can.
services.expect: Dr. Vernon will ask about your symptoms, health history, medicines, and family history. You will likely have a physical exam, which may include an exam of the belly. Depending on your needs, the doctor may order blood work, stool tests, imaging, or a procedure. Plan for the visit to take some time, especially if it is your first one.
services.after: You will leave with a plan, which may include tests, procedures, medicines, or lifestyle changes. The office will help schedule any procedures and give you prep instructions. Dr. Vernon will follow up with you on test results and next steps.

conditions.name: Heartburn / acid reflux
conditions.text: Stomach acid backs up into the esophagus, causing burning in the chest or throat, a sour taste or a cough. Frequent reflux (GERD) can damage the esophagus over time.
conditions.what: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest or throat. It happens when stomach acid flows back up into the esophagus, the tube that carries food from your mouth to your stomach. When this happens often, it is called gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD. Over time, frequent reflux can irritate and damage the lining of the esophagus.
conditions.causes:
A weak or relaxed valve between the esophagus and stomach
Large meals or lying down soon after eating
Extra body weight or pregnancy
A hiatal hernia
Smoking and alcohol
Certain foods, such as spicy, fatty, or acidic foods, chocolate, or caffeine
conditions.symptoms:
Burning pain in the chest, often after eating or at night
Sour or bitter taste in the mouth
Food or liquid coming back up
Chronic cough or hoarse voice
Sore throat or a feeling of a lump in the throat
Trouble sleeping because of symptoms
conditions.treatment: Many people start with changes to diet, meal timing, and sleep position, along with medicines that lower or block stomach acid. If symptoms last, come back often, or include warning signs, Dr. Vernon may recommend an upper endoscopy (EGD) to look at the esophagus and stomach. This test can find inflammation, narrowing, or changes in the lining such as Barrett's esophagus. Your treatment plan is based on what is found and how you respond. Some patients with severe reflux may need a referral to a surgeon.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have heartburn more than twice a week or it does not get better with treatment. Get care right away for trouble or pain with swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools, weight loss you can't explain, or chest pain that could be your heart.

conditions.name: Colon cancer
conditions.text: Cancer of the large intestine, usually starting as a small growth called a polyp. Caught early, it is one of the most treatable cancers.
conditions.what: Colon cancer is cancer that starts in the large intestine (colon) or rectum. It most often begins as a small growth called a polyp. Some polyps can turn into cancer slowly over several years. Finding and removing polyps early is one of the best ways to prevent colon cancer.
conditions.causes:
Age, with risk rising over time
A personal or family history of colon cancer or polyps
Inflammatory bowel disease, such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis
Certain inherited genetic conditions
Smoking, heavy alcohol use, and extra body weight
A diet high in red or processed meat and low in fiber
conditions.symptoms:
Often no symptoms in the early stages
Blood in or on the stool
A change in bowel habits that lasts, such as diarrhea, constipation, or narrow stools
Belly pain or cramping that does not go away
Feeling tired or weak, which can be from anemia
Weight loss you can't explain
conditions.treatment: Colon cancer is usually found with a colonoscopy, where polyps can be removed and tissue samples (biopsies) can be taken. If cancer is found, more tests help show how far it has spread. Treatment often includes surgery and may include chemotherapy or radiation, so you may need a referral to a surgeon and a cancer specialist. Dr. Vernon can help coordinate your care and follow-up exams.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you see blood in your stool, have a change in bowel habits that lasts more than a few weeks, or have ongoing belly pain or weight loss you can't explain. Do not wait for symptoms to get screened.

conditions.name: Colon cancer screening
conditions.text: Tests that find colon cancer, or the polyps that can become cancer, before symptoms start. Options include colonoscopy and stool tests like Cologuard®; most adults should begin at 45.
conditions.what: Colon cancer screening means checking for cancer or polyps before you have any symptoms. Screening can find polyps so they can be removed before they turn into cancer. It can also find cancer early, when it is often easier to treat. There are several screening options, and your doctor can help you pick the right one.
conditions.causes:
Reaching age 45 or older
A family history of colon cancer or polyps
A personal history of polyps or colon cancer
Inflammatory bowel disease
Certain inherited genetic conditions
conditions.symptoms:
Screening is meant for people with no symptoms
Most polyps and early cancers cause no symptoms
If you do have symptoms, such as bleeding or a change in bowel habits, you need a diagnostic exam, not just screening
conditions.treatment: Colonoscopy is the most complete screening test because it lets the doctor see the whole colon and remove polyps during the same exam. The practice also offers Cologuard, a stool DNA test you do at home, for some average-risk adults. A positive stool test needs a follow-up colonoscopy. How often you need screening depends on your test results and personal risk.
conditions.when: Adults at average risk should start screening at age 45. People with a family history, a history of polyps, or inflammatory bowel disease may need to start earlier and be screened more often, so talk with the doctor about your risk.

conditions.name: Obesity
conditions.text: Excess body weight that raises the risk of fatty liver, reflux, diabetes and colon cancer. We help with nutrition and lifestyle plans as part of your digestive care.
conditions.what: Obesity means having more body fat than is healthy for your body. It is a long-term health condition, not a lack of willpower. Extra weight can affect the digestive system and raise the risk of problems such as acid reflux, fatty liver disease, gallstones, and some cancers.
conditions.causes:
Eating more calories than the body uses over time
Low physical activity
Genetics and family history
Some medicines and health conditions
Poor sleep and stress
Environment and daily habits
conditions.symptoms:
Higher body weight or waist size
Heartburn or acid reflux
Shortness of breath with activity
Joint or back pain
Feeling tired often
Snoring or sleep problems
conditions.treatment: Care starts with a full health review, including your weight history, eating habits, medicines, and related conditions. Dr. Vernon's practice offers nutrition and lifestyle wellness guidance to help you set realistic goals for food, activity, and sleep. Your doctor may order blood tests or imaging to check for weight-related problems such as fatty liver. Some patients may also benefit from medicines or a referral to a weight-loss surgeon. Small, steady changes can improve health over time.
conditions.when: Talk with the doctor if your weight is affecting your health or daily life, or if you have reflux, belly pain, or abnormal liver tests. Call sooner if you have sudden weight changes you can't explain.

conditions.name: Fatty liver
conditions.text: Fat builds up in the liver, often linked to weight, diabetes or alcohol. It usually has no symptoms but can lead to inflammation and scarring if not managed.
conditions.what: Fatty liver disease happens when too much fat builds up in the liver. The most common type is linked to extra weight, diabetes, and high cholesterol rather than alcohol. It is now often called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). In some people, the fat causes inflammation that can lead to scarring of the liver over time.
conditions.causes:
Extra body weight, especially around the belly
Type 2 diabetes or prediabetes
High cholesterol or triglycerides
High blood pressure
Heavy alcohol use
Certain medicines
conditions.symptoms:
Often no symptoms
Feeling tired
Mild discomfort in the upper right belly
Abnormal liver blood tests found on routine labs
Yellow skin or eyes, or belly swelling, in advanced disease
conditions.treatment: Fatty liver is often found on blood tests or imaging done for another reason. Dr. Vernon may order blood work, an ultrasound, or other tests to check how much the liver is affected and whether there is scarring. The main treatment is lifestyle change, including gradual weight loss, healthy eating, regular activity, and limiting alcohol. The practice offers nutrition and lifestyle wellness guidance to support these changes. Managing diabetes, cholesterol, and blood pressure also helps protect the liver.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have abnormal liver tests or risk factors such as diabetes or extra weight. Get care right away if you notice yellow skin or eyes, belly swelling, confusion, or vomiting blood.

conditions.name: Ulcers / gallstones
conditions.text: Ulcers are sores in the lining of the stomach or small intestine, often from H. pylori or pain relievers like ibuprofen. Gallstones are hard deposits in the gallbladder that can cause pain after meals.
conditions.what: A peptic ulcer is an open sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. Gallstones are hard pieces that form in the gallbladder, a small organ under the liver that stores bile. Both can cause pain in the upper belly, so they are often looked at together. They have different causes and treatments.
conditions.causes:
Ulcers: infection with H. pylori bacteria
Ulcers: regular use of pain relievers such as aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen
Ulcers: smoking and heavy alcohol use
Gallstones: too much cholesterol or bilirubin in the bile
Gallstones: extra weight, rapid weight loss, pregnancy, or family history
conditions.symptoms:
Burning or gnawing pain in the upper belly
Pain after fatty meals, often in the upper right belly or back (gallstones)
Nausea or vomiting
Bloating or feeling full quickly
Dark or black stools (ulcers)
Fever or yellow skin or eyes (gallstone problems)
conditions.treatment: For possible ulcers, Dr. Vernon may perform an upper endoscopy (EGD) to look at the stomach lining, take biopsies, and check for H. pylori. Ulcers are usually treated with medicines that lower stomach acid, along with antibiotics if H. pylori is present. Gallstones are usually found with an ultrasound. Gallstones that cause symptoms are often treated by removing the gallbladder, so you may need a referral to a surgeon. Avoiding certain pain relievers can help ulcers heal and keep them from coming back.
conditions.when: Call the doctor for ongoing upper belly pain or pain after meals. Get emergency care for severe belly pain, vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, fever with belly pain, or yellow skin or eyes.

conditions.name: Abdominal pain
conditions.text: Pain or cramping in the belly can come from many digestive causes. We find the source with a careful exam and the right tests.
conditions.what: Abdominal pain is pain anywhere between the chest and the groin. It can be sharp, dull, crampy, or burning, and it may come and go or stay constant. Many different digestive problems can cause belly pain. Finding the cause is the first step to the right treatment.
conditions.causes:
Gas, constipation, or indigestion
Acid reflux, ulcers, or gastritis
Gallstones or pancreas problems
Irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease
Infections or food intolerances
Diverticulitis or other colon problems
conditions.symptoms:
Cramping or aching in the belly
Bloating or swelling
Nausea or vomiting
Diarrhea or constipation
Pain that changes with eating or bowel movements
Fever or loss of appetite
conditions.treatment: Dr. Vernon will ask about where the pain is, when it happens, and what makes it better or worse, and will do a physical exam. Based on your history, you may need blood work, stool tests, imaging, an upper endoscopy (EGD), or a colonoscopy. In some cases, capsule endoscopy may be used to look at the small intestine. Treatment depends on the cause and may include diet changes, medicines, or further care. Some causes may need a referral to a surgeon.
conditions.when: Call the doctor for belly pain that lasts more than a few days, keeps coming back, or comes with weight loss or changes in bowel habits. Get emergency care for sudden severe pain, a hard or tender belly, vomiting blood, bloody or black stools, high fever, or pain during pregnancy.

conditions.name: Intestinal bleeding
conditions.text: Bleeding anywhere in the digestive tract, which may show up as black or bloody stool, or as anemia (low blood count). It always deserves an evaluation.
conditions.what: Intestinal bleeding, also called gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding, is bleeding anywhere in the digestive tract. It can come from the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, colon, or rectum. Bleeding may be easy to see or so slow that it is only found through a blood test showing low iron or anemia. GI bleeding is a sign of a problem that needs to be checked.
conditions.causes:
Ulcers or inflammation in the stomach or esophagus
Hemorrhoids or small tears near the anus
Diverticulosis
Polyps or colon cancer
Inflammatory bowel disease
Abnormal blood vessels in the lining of the gut
conditions.symptoms:
Bright red blood in or on the stool
Black, tarry stools
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Feeling tired, weak, or short of breath
Dizziness or pale skin
Low iron or anemia on blood tests
conditions.treatment: Finding the source of the bleeding is key. Dr. Vernon may use an upper endoscopy (EGD) to check the esophagus, stomach, and upper small intestine, and a colonoscopy to check the colon and rectum. If those tests do not show the cause, capsule endoscopy can look at the small intestine. Many sources of bleeding can be treated during endoscopy. Treatment may also include medicines and iron replacement, depending on the cause.
conditions.when: Call the doctor for any blood in your stool or low iron on blood tests. Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you are vomiting blood, have large amounts of blood or black stools, or feel faint, dizzy, or short of breath.

conditions.name: Difficulty swallowing
conditions.text: Food that feels stuck, or pain when swallowing (dysphagia). It can come from a narrowed esophagus, reflux or muscle problems, and is often treatable with dilation.
conditions.what: Difficulty swallowing, called dysphagia, means it takes more effort or time to move food or liquid from your mouth to your stomach. Some people feel like food is stuck in the throat or chest. It can be caused by a narrowing in the esophagus or by problems with the muscles and nerves that control swallowing. It should always be checked by a doctor.
conditions.causes:
Narrowing of the esophagus from long-term acid reflux
Eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergy-related inflammation
A ring or web in the esophagus
Muscle or nerve problems that affect swallowing
Tumors of the esophagus
Infections or inflammation of the esophagus
conditions.symptoms:
Feeling of food sticking in the throat or chest
Pain when swallowing
Coughing or choking while eating or drinking
Food or liquid coming back up
Heartburn
Weight loss or avoiding certain foods
conditions.treatment: Dr. Vernon will ask about your symptoms, such as whether trouble happens with solids, liquids, or both. An upper endoscopy (EGD) is often used to look at the esophagus and take biopsies. If a narrowing is found, the esophagus can often be gently stretched during the same procedure with esophageal dilation. Treatment may also include medicines for reflux or inflammation. Other tests or referrals may be needed depending on the cause.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have trouble swallowing, even if it comes and goes. Get emergency care if food is stuck and you cannot swallow your saliva, or if you have trouble breathing.

conditions.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
conditions.text: A common condition causing cramping, bloating, gas, diarrhea or constipation without visible damage to the bowel. Diet, stress management and medication can help.
conditions.what: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common long-term condition that affects how the gut works. It causes belly pain along with changes in bowel habits, such as diarrhea, constipation, or both. IBS does not damage the intestines or cause cancer. Symptoms can come and go and often improve with treatment.
conditions.causes:
Changes in how the gut and brain communicate
A gut that is extra sensitive to stretching or gas
Changes in how fast food moves through the intestines
A past stomach or intestinal infection
Stress and anxiety, which can make symptoms worse
Certain foods that trigger symptoms
conditions.symptoms:
Belly pain or cramping, often related to bowel movements
Bloating and gas
Diarrhea, constipation, or both
Mucus in the stool
Feeling that a bowel movement is not finished
conditions.treatment: IBS is diagnosed based on your symptoms and by ruling out other conditions. Dr. Vernon may order blood tests, stool tests, or a colonoscopy, especially if you have warning signs or are due for screening. Treatment often starts with diet changes, such as adjusting fiber or trying a low-FODMAP plan, along with stress management and regular exercise. The practice's nutrition and lifestyle guidance can help you find your triggers. Medicines may also help control pain, diarrhea, or constipation.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have ongoing changes in bowel habits or belly pain. Call sooner if you have rectal bleeding, weight loss you can't explain, fever, symptoms that wake you up at night, or symptoms that start after age 50.

conditions.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
conditions.text: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis: long-term inflammation of the digestive tract that causes diarrhea, pain and bleeding. Ongoing treatment keeps it under control.
conditions.what: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of long-term conditions that cause inflammation in the digestive tract. The two main types are Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn's disease can affect any part of the digestive tract, while ulcerative colitis affects the colon and rectum. IBD often has periods of flares and periods of calm.
conditions.causes:
An immune system that attacks the lining of the gut
Genetics and family history
Environmental factors
Smoking, which raises the risk of Crohn's disease
The exact cause is not fully known
conditions.symptoms:
Diarrhea that lasts or keeps coming back
Belly pain and cramping
Blood or mucus in the stool
An urgent need to have a bowel movement
Feeling tired
Weight loss or poor appetite
Fever during flares
conditions.treatment: IBD is usually diagnosed with a colonoscopy and biopsies, along with blood tests, stool tests, and sometimes imaging. Capsule endoscopy may be used to check the small intestine for Crohn's disease. Treatment uses medicines that calm the inflammation and help keep the disease in remission. Dr. Vernon works with you on a long-term plan and regular monitoring, including colonoscopy to check for changes in the colon lining. Some patients may need a referral to a surgeon or other specialists.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have diarrhea, belly pain, or blood in your stool that lasts more than a few days. Get care right away for heavy bleeding, severe belly pain, high fever, or signs of dehydration.

conditions.name: Liver disease
conditions.text: Any condition that harms the liver, including fatty liver, hepatitis and cirrhosis (scarring). Early diagnosis helps protect liver function.
conditions.what: Liver disease is any condition that harms the liver. The liver filters the blood, helps digest food, stores energy, and makes important proteins. Over time, ongoing damage can cause scarring called fibrosis and, in later stages, cirrhosis. Many liver problems can be managed, especially when found early.
conditions.causes:
Fatty liver disease linked to weight, diabetes, or cholesterol
Viral hepatitis, such as hepatitis B or C
Heavy alcohol use
Certain medicines, supplements, or toxins
Autoimmune liver disease
Inherited conditions, such as too much iron in the body
conditions.symptoms:
Often no symptoms early on
Feeling tired or weak
Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
Swelling in the belly or legs
Dark urine or pale stools
Itchy skin
Easy bruising or bleeding
conditions.treatment: Liver disease is often found through blood tests that show abnormal liver numbers. Dr. Vernon may order more blood work, an ultrasound, or other tests to find the cause and check for scarring. Treatment depends on the cause and may include lifestyle changes, stopping alcohol, treating viral hepatitis, or adjusting medicines. Patients with cirrhosis may need an upper endoscopy (EGD) to check for enlarged veins in the esophagus. Some patients may need a referral to a liver specialist.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have abnormal liver tests, yellow skin or eyes, or swelling in the belly or legs. Get emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, confusion, or severe belly pain.

conditions.name: Hemorrhoids
conditions.text: Swollen veins around the rectum or anus that can itch, hurt or bleed. Most can be treated in the office with quick, minimally invasive banding.
conditions.what: Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in the lower rectum and anus. Internal hemorrhoids are inside the rectum and are often painless, but they can bleed. External hemorrhoids are under the skin around the anus and can be itchy or painful. Hemorrhoids are very common and treatable.
conditions.causes:
Straining during bowel movements
Long-term constipation or diarrhea
Sitting on the toilet for long periods
Pregnancy
Extra body weight
A low-fiber diet
conditions.symptoms:
Bright red blood on toilet paper or in the toilet
Itching or irritation around the anus
Pain or discomfort, especially when sitting
A lump or swelling near the anus
Tissue that bulges out during bowel movements
conditions.treatment: Dr. Vernon can usually diagnose hemorrhoids with an exam in the office. Mild hemorrhoids often improve with more fiber, more water, and less straining. For internal hemorrhoids that keep causing problems, the practice offers in-office banding with the CRH O'Regan System. This method uses a small rubber band to cut off blood flow to the hemorrhoid so it shrinks and falls off. Because bleeding can also come from other causes, a colonoscopy may be recommended, and some patients may need a referral to a surgeon.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have rectal bleeding, even if you think it is from hemorrhoids, or if home care does not help within a week. Get care right away for heavy bleeding, severe pain, or dizziness.

conditions.name: Rectal bleeding
conditions.text: Blood on toilet paper, in the bowl or in the stool. It is often from hemorrhoids, but it can be a sign of polyps or cancer, so it should be checked.
conditions.what: Rectal bleeding is blood that passes from the anus. You may see bright red blood on toilet paper, in the toilet, or mixed with stool. It often comes from a problem in the lower colon or rectum. Rectal bleeding should always be checked by a doctor.
conditions.causes:
Hemorrhoids
Anal fissures, which are small tears in the lining of the anus
Diverticulosis
Polyps or colon cancer
Inflammatory bowel disease
Infections of the colon
conditions.symptoms:
Bright red blood on toilet paper or in the toilet bowl
Blood mixed in with the stool
Dark red or maroon stools
Pain or itching around the anus
Changes in bowel habits
Feeling tired or dizzy if bleeding is heavy
conditions.treatment: Dr. Vernon will ask about your symptoms and do an exam. Depending on your age and history, you may need a flexible sigmoidoscopy or a full colonoscopy to find the source of the bleeding. Many causes can be treated, and polyps can often be removed during colonoscopy. If hemorrhoids are the cause, the practice offers in-office banding with the CRH O'Regan System. Treatment depends on what is found.
conditions.when: Call the doctor for any rectal bleeding. Call 911 or go to the emergency room for heavy bleeding, large clots, or if you feel faint, dizzy, or have a fast heartbeat.

conditions.name: Constipation
conditions.text: Infrequent, hard or difficult bowel movements. Usually managed with diet, fluids and medication, but a lasting change in bowel habits should be evaluated.
conditions.what: Constipation means having bowel movements less often than usual or having stools that are hard, dry, or hard to pass. Many people have constipation from time to time. When it lasts for weeks or longer, it is called chronic constipation. It can usually be improved with changes in diet and habits, but sometimes it points to another problem.
conditions.causes:
Not enough fiber or water in the diet
Low physical activity
Ignoring the urge to have a bowel movement
Certain medicines, such as some pain medicines and iron pills
Irritable bowel syndrome or pelvic floor problems
Thyroid problems, diabetes, or other health conditions
conditions.symptoms:
Fewer than three bowel movements a week
Hard or lumpy stools
Straining during bowel movements
Feeling like you can't fully empty your bowels
Bloating or belly discomfort
conditions.treatment: Dr. Vernon will review your diet, medicines, and bowel habits and may order blood tests. A colonoscopy may be recommended if you have warning signs or are due for colon cancer screening. Treatment often starts with more fiber, more fluids, and regular exercise. The practice's nutrition and lifestyle guidance can help you build these habits. Your doctor may also suggest laxatives, stool softeners, or other medicines when needed.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if constipation lasts more than a few weeks or is a new change for you. Get care sooner for blood in your stool, weight loss you can't explain, severe belly pain, vomiting, or being unable to pass gas.

conditions.name: Hepatitis
conditions.text: Inflammation of the liver, most often from a virus (hepatitis B or C), alcohol or an autoimmune condition. Many types can be treated or cured.
conditions.what: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. It is often caused by a virus, most commonly hepatitis A, B, or C. It can also be caused by alcohol, certain medicines, or the immune system attacking the liver. Some types clear up on their own, while others can last for years and damage the liver if not treated.
conditions.causes:
Hepatitis A: contaminated food or water
Hepatitis B: blood, sexual contact, or from mother to baby at birth
Hepatitis C: blood contact, such as shared needles
Heavy alcohol use
Certain medicines or supplements
Autoimmune hepatitis
conditions.symptoms:
Often no symptoms, especially with long-term hepatitis B or C
Feeling tired
Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
Dark urine or pale stools
Nausea or poor appetite
Pain in the upper right belly
conditions.treatment: Hepatitis is diagnosed with blood tests that check liver function and look for viruses. Dr. Vernon may also order an ultrasound or other tests to check for liver scarring. Hepatitis C can often be cured with antiviral medicines, and hepatitis B can be controlled with medicine when needed. Other types are treated based on the cause, such as stopping alcohol or a medicine. Vaccines can prevent hepatitis A and B, so ask if you are protected.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have abnormal liver tests, have been exposed to hepatitis, or have yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or ongoing tiredness. Ask about one-time hepatitis C testing for adults and about hepatitis B testing if you have risk factors.

conditions.name: Diverticulosis
conditions.text: Small pouches that form in the wall of the colon, common with age. They can become inflamed (diverticulitis) or bleed.
conditions.what: Diverticulosis means having small pouches, called diverticula, that bulge out through weak spots in the wall of the colon. It is common, especially as people get older. Most people with diverticulosis have no symptoms. When the pouches become inflamed or infected, it is called diverticulitis.
conditions.causes:
Getting older
A low-fiber diet
Long-term constipation and straining
Low physical activity
Extra body weight and smoking
conditions.symptoms:
Usually no symptoms
Bloating or mild cramping
Changes in bowel habits
Painless rectal bleeding, which can sometimes be heavy
With diverticulitis: belly pain, often on the lower left side, fever, and nausea
conditions.treatment: Diverticulosis is often found during a colonoscopy or on a CT scan done for another reason. A high-fiber diet, plenty of fluids, and regular exercise may help prevent problems. Diverticulitis is often confirmed with a CT scan and may be treated with rest, diet changes, and sometimes antibiotics. Dr. Vernon may recommend a colonoscopy after a flare has healed to check the colon. Some people with repeated or severe flares may need a referral to a surgeon.
conditions.when: Call the doctor for belly pain that lasts, fever, or changes in bowel habits. Get emergency care for severe belly pain, high fever, vomiting, or heavy rectal bleeding.

conditions.name: Helicobacter pylori
conditions.text: A common stomach bacteria that can cause ulcers, gastritis and indigestion. It is found with a simple test and treated with antibiotics.
conditions.what: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a type of bacteria that can live in the lining of the stomach. Many people carry it without knowing. In some people, it causes inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis) and ulcers. Long-term infection also raises the risk of stomach cancer, so treating it is important.
conditions.causes:
Spread through saliva, vomit, or stool
Contaminated food or water
Crowded living conditions
Often picked up in childhood
More common in some parts of the world
conditions.symptoms:
Often no symptoms
Burning or aching pain in the upper belly
Bloating or burping
Nausea
Poor appetite or feeling full quickly
Black stools if an ulcer bleeds
conditions.treatment: H. pylori can be found with a breath test, stool test, or with biopsies taken during an upper endoscopy (EGD). Treatment usually combines two or more antibiotics with a medicine that lowers stomach acid, taken for about two weeks. It is important to take every dose exactly as prescribed. Dr. Vernon will usually recheck with a breath or stool test after treatment to make sure the infection is gone. Some acid medicines need to be stopped before testing, so follow the office's instructions.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have ongoing upper belly pain, indigestion, or a history of ulcers. Get care right away for vomiting blood, black stools, or weight loss you can't explain.

conditions.name: Unexplained weight loss
conditions.text: Losing weight without trying can signal a digestive problem, such as poor absorption of nutrients, and should always be evaluated.
conditions.what: Unexplained weight loss is losing weight without trying, such as without changing your diet or activity. Losing a noticeable amount of weight over several months without a clear reason should be checked by a doctor. It can be a sign of a problem in the digestive system or elsewhere in the body.
conditions.causes:
Problems absorbing nutrients, such as celiac disease
Inflammatory bowel disease
Ulcers or trouble swallowing that make eating hard
Cancers of the digestive tract or other organs
Thyroid problems or diabetes
Depression, medicines, or dental problems
conditions.symptoms:
Losing weight without trying
Poor appetite or feeling full quickly
Feeling tired or weak
Changes in bowel habits
Belly pain, nausea, or vomiting
Trouble swallowing
conditions.treatment: Dr. Vernon will review your health history, medicines, and diet and do a physical exam. Testing often starts with blood work and may include imaging. Depending on your symptoms, you may need an upper endoscopy (EGD), a colonoscopy, or capsule endoscopy to look for problems in the digestive tract. Treatment depends on the cause. The practice's nutrition guidance can also help you regain and keep a healthy weight.
conditions.when: Call the doctor if you have lost weight without trying over the past several months. Call sooner if weight loss comes with trouble swallowing, vomiting, blood in your stool, black stools, or ongoing belly pain.

faqs.q: What is a colonoscopy, and why is it important?
faqs.a: A colonoscopy examines the inside of your colon for polyps, abnormalities or signs of colon cancer. It is the only test that can both detect and prevent colon cancer, because polyps can be removed during the procedure.

In a study of 10,000 average-risk people, Cologuard found 92% of colon cancers. It is non-invasive and needs no prep, but it does not reliably find precancerous polyps, and a positive result needs a follow-up colonoscopy. [Read more about Cologuard](article.html?id=cologuard).

faqs.q: What should I expect during a flexible sigmoidoscopy?
faqs.a: It is a quick, minimally invasive screening of the lower colon. It typically takes less than 30 minutes and needs minimal preparation.
Endoscopy is very safe when performed by experienced specialists. Risks are small; some patients have minor discomfort afterward. Our team looks after your safety throughout.

faqs.q: How do I prepare for my procedure?
faqs.a: It depends on the procedure. A colonoscopy requires a clear-liquid diet and bowel prep. We'll give you instructions for your procedure, and you can download the [colonoscopy prep instructions](patients.html#prep) here.
We accept Medicare, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Cigna, Aetna, UnitedHealthcare, Wellpath and many others. Please call (919) 577-0085 to confirm your coverage.

organs.name: Stomach
organs.text: A J-shaped organ just left of center, between the esophagus and the small intestine. Protein digestion begins here.

organs.name: Small intestine
organs.text: Folded into much of the abdomen, it does most of the digestion and absorption of nutrients. Enzymes and bile break food into small building blocks that pass into the bloodstream. The duodenum is its first, C-shaped section.

organs.name: Colon
organs.text: The large intestine wraps around the small intestine like a frame. It absorbs water from what's left of digested food and moves waste out of the body.

organs.name: Rectum
organs.text: The last 6–8 inches of the large intestine. It holds stool until it leaves the body.

organs.name: Liver
organs.text: The largest internal organ. It stores vitamins, sugars and fats and releases them as needed; builds the proteins that clot blood and make new cells; filters waste from the blood; and breaks down harmful substances like alcohol.

organs.name: Gallbladder
organs.text: A small organ under the liver on the right side. It stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the intestine to help digest fats.

organs.name: Pancreas
organs.text: A fish-shaped organ behind the stomach. It makes hormones like insulin and glucagon, and digestive enzymes that it sends to the small intestine.

quiz.title: Colon Cancer Risk Quiz
quiz.intro: Are you at risk for colon cancer? Gastrointestinal problems account for more hospitalizations in the U.S. than any other group of disorders. Answer these quick questions to see whether you should talk with us about screening. Your answers stay on your device.
questions: Have you had colon polyps or colon cancer before?
Has a parent, sibling or child had colon polyps or colon cancer?
Have you had diarrhea or constipation for more than 3 weeks?
Do you have a family history of pancreatic, breast or uterine cancer?
Have you seen any blood in or on your stool?
Have you had unexplained weight loss?
Do you have familial polyposis syndrome?
Do you have unexplained abdominal pain?
quiz.yesResult: Based on your answers, you may benefit from colon cancer screening or an evaluation. Please call us to schedule a visit with Dr. Vernon.
quiz.noResult: You answered no to every question. Keep up with routine checkups, and call us if anything changes. Any screening is better than none.

articles.title: Cologuard technology
articles.summary: A no-prep, no-sedation screening option for colon cancer, and how it compares to colonoscopy.
articles.body:
Testing for colon cancer just got easier. Cologuard is a colon cancer screening test that is simple to use. It involves no prep, no sedation, and most importantly, it's effective.

## What exactly is Cologuard?
Cologuard tests for genetic changes in stool that are associated with colon cancer. It correctly identifies 92% of people who have colon cancer. It will not, however, lower your risk of developing cancer, because it cannot reliably detect precancerous polyps. If a Cologuard test comes back positive, a follow-up colonoscopy will be recommended.

## How does it work?
DNA is continuously shed from cells in the intestinal lining into stool. If cancer or precancer is present, abnormal cells are shed along with normal ones. Cologuard looks for altered DNA and/or blood in the stool that may signal cancer or precancer.

## How effective is it?
In a study of 10,000 people at average risk for colon cancer, Cologuard found 92% of cancers. It was negative in 87% of people without the disease.

## Should colonoscopy be used as well?
Cologuard is a screening test. Any positive result should be discussed with your doctor and followed by a diagnostic colonoscopy.

## The bottom line
Colon cancer is common. Colonoscopy is the only test proven to both detect and prevent colon cancer, because precancerous polyps are removed during the procedure. About one in three patients has polyps removed during a colonoscopy. For people who don't want a colonoscopy, Cologuard is one alternative.

Remember: any colon cancer screening test is better than none. Learn more at [cologuard.com](https://www.cologuard.com/).

articles.title: What is an endoscopy?
articles.summary: How an endoscope lets your doctor see inside your digestive tract, and why it might be recommended.
articles.body:
An endoscopy is a nonsurgical procedure that lets your doctor look inside your digestive tract with a thin camera called an endoscope. In an upper endoscopy, the endoscope passes through the mouth and throat to view the esophagus, stomach and first part of the small intestine. It is usually a quick outpatient procedure.

An endoscope can also view the large intestine (the colon) through the rectum. Your physician may recommend an endoscopy to evaluate:

- Stomach problems or pain
- Bowel pain or diarrhea
- Other digestive tract problems
- Ulcers
- Polyps, growths or other colon findings

Sometimes your physician will take a small tissue sample (a biopsy) during the procedure to check for disease. Ask your doctor to explain as much as possible beforehand so you're prepared.

If you have questions about an endoscopy or a related procedure, please call our office.

articles.title: Dr. Vernon receives BCBSNC Tier 1 recognition
articles.summary: Our practice received a Tier 1 Designation from Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina for high quality and cost efficiency.
articles.body:
The practice of Kurt Vernon, MD, The GI Guy, is proud to announce that we have received a Tier 1 Designation, a high-quality recognition from one of the nation's largest health insurers, [Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina](https://www.bluecrossnc.com/).

The BCBSNC Tiered Network uses claims data to identify high-quality, low-cost providers and help consumers make more informed choices about their care. Our practice was scored on gastroenterology quality measures, including colonoscopy and GERD care.

"It is a pleasure to be recognized by BCBSNC as a Tier 1 North Carolina gastroenterologist. We will continue to improve upon our quality measures to provide the best care for our patients," said Dr. Vernon.

The designation compares physician performance with peers on nationally accepted quality measures and local cost-efficiency benchmarks, within the same region and specialty. Practices that exceed both the quality and cost thresholds are designated Tier 1.

fasttrack.title: Positive Cologuard® or stool test? Get your colonoscopy in 7–14 days.
fasttrack.intro: A positive stool test doesn't mean you have cancer, but the only way to know is a colonoscopy. In many places that means waiting months, and the waiting is the hardest part. With Fast-Track, we usually schedule your colonoscopy within 7–14 days of your phone screening.
fasttrack.noVisit: No office visit needed first. If you're generally healthy, we screen you by phone, send your prep instructions and schedule your procedure.

steps.title: Call us
steps.text: Tell us you had a positive Cologuard®, FIT or other stool test. Have your result, insurance card and medication list handy.

steps.title: Phone screening
steps.text: Our staff asks a short list of health questions. If you're healthy enough for a direct colonoscopy, you skip the separate office visit.

steps.title: Prep instructions
steps.text: We send your bowel prep instructions: exactly what to buy, eat and drink before your procedure.

steps.title: Your colonoscopy
steps.text: Dr. Vernon performs your colonoscopy, usually within 7–14 days, and goes over the results with you.

fasttrack.fit:
You had a positive (abnormal) Cologuard®, FIT or other stool-based colon cancer test
You're generally healthy
You'd rather not wait months to find out
fasttrack.notFit:
Take blood thinners such as warfarin, Eliquis, Xarelto or Plavix
Have serious heart, lung or kidney disease
Have had problems with anesthesia or sedation
Have symptoms like heavy bleeding or severe abdominal pain
fasttrack.notFitNote: That doesn't rule you out. It just means Dr. Vernon reviews your history first. Our staff will tell you on the call.
fasttrack.bring:
Your positive test result (or the name of the doctor who ordered it)
Your insurance card
A list of your medications
A driver for the day of your procedure
fasttrack.insurance: Many insurance plans, including Medicare, now treat a colonoscopy after a positive stool test as part of screening, which can mean little or no out-of-pocket cost. Coverage varies, so our staff will check your plan when you call.

faqs.q: Does a positive stool test mean I have cancer?
faqs.a: No. Most people with a positive stool test do not have cancer. The test can be positive because of polyps, hemorrhoids or other causes. A colonoscopy is the only way to know, and polyps found during it can be removed on the spot.

faqs.q: Why do I need a colonoscopy if I already did a stool test?
faqs.a: A stool test only tells us something may be there. A colonoscopy lets Dr. Vernon see the whole colon and remove polyps before they can turn into cancer.
Some insurance plans require one. If yours does, we can request it from the doctor who ordered your stool test.

faqs.q: I don't live near Fuquay-Varina or Dunn. Can I still come?
faqs.a: Yes. Patients come to us from across North Carolina so they don't have to wait. Most people only make one trip, on the day of the procedure.

faqs.q: How fast can I be seen?
faqs.a: We usually schedule your colonoscopy within 7–14 days of your phone screening, depending on your health history, your insurance and your prep.

fasttrack.providers: If your patient has a positive stool test and is facing a long wait, send them our way. Fax the referral and the stool test result to (910) 891-5323, and we'll call your patient to complete the phone screening. We send the colonoscopy and pathology reports back to you.
fasttrack.homeBand: **Positive Cologuard® or stool test?** Get your colonoscopy in 7–14 days. No office visit needed first.
